name: Lupine
lede: Lupine is a soft, slightly greyed blue named for the lupine flower, recorded by the Maerz and Paul dictionary in 1930 with a first use in 1922.

sections.title: A flower spike, not a pigment
sections.body:
Our data traces the name to the lupine, the flowering plant, rather than a pigment or a place [1]. The Maerz and Paul dictionary of 1930 plots it on plate 34 D7 and gives it a first recorded use of 1922, and the ISCC-NBS system of 1955 files the same area as block 181, "light blue" [1]. In LCH terms it reads as lightness 67, chroma 22, hue 263 degrees: soft, moderately saturated, and leaning a little purple of true blue [1].

The same Maerz and Paul plate carries two other names for nearby shades: Zenith, first recorded in 1892, and Blue Lotus, in 1923 [2]. Lupine's nearest computed neighbor is [[iceberg|Iceberg]], 4.1 units off and more vivid, followed by [[air-superiority-blue|Air Superiority Blue]] and [[watteau|Watteau]] [3]. The closest everyday name is [[cornflower]], about 7.4 units away [4].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a close match covers enough of the canvas in 164, as photographed (110 by the stricter within-painting measure), which makes it more common than 60 percent of the named colors we track [5]. It peaks in paintings from the 1800s, at 1.2 times the rate expected from that century's share of the archive (51 of 8,345 paintings) [5]. Inside a painting it most often plays a hidden color, in 30 percent of its matches, by lightness rank within the canvas; varnish cannot fake that ranking [5]. [[painter:alfred-sisley|Alfred Sisley]] used it most: it appears in 4 of his 50 works here, 5.5 times the rate of the museums those works come from [5]. The earliest match is a 1440 painting by Rogier van der Weyden, 490 years before the name's first record in 1930, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [5].
